questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Money as exchange and as store of value
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the exchange role of money from its store of value role
questions.stem: Money serves as a medium of exchange when it settles a purchase today, and as a store of value when it can be held back for later spending. Which situation shows the second role rather than the first?

options.text: A household keeps a standing balance in a deposit account through a year of purchases
A shopper pays a shopkeeper with banknotes so that the sale can be completed today
options.misconception: treats a payment made today as evidence of a store of value

options.text: A worker hands a five unit note to a bus driver in exchange for a ticket
options.misconception: labels a single payment as deferred purchasing power

options.text: A wholesaler settles an invoice the same afternoon it reaches a retailer
options.misconception: believes same day settlement shows money being held over time

questions.explanation: The store of value role is about purchasing power carried forward, and a balance left sitting in an account across a year of purchases is exactly that: money not consumed on goods today, so it can buy goods tomorrow. The other three cases all settle a liability immediately, which is the exchange role and nothing more. A note handed over for a ticket is spent the moment it changes hands, and same day settlement is the opposite of deferral, so neither demonstrates deferred purchasing power at all.
questions.hint: Ask which case involves money surviving the purchase it could have paid for.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: name the standard functions money performs
questions.stem: Which set of roles is the standard set of functions that money performs in an economy?

options.text: Medium of exchange, unit of account, and store of value
Means of production, source of household income, and store of value
options.misconception: replaces exchange and unit of account with production and income

options.text: Unit of account, store of value, and distributor of goods to households
options.misconception: lists a distribution role that money does not perform

options.text: Medium of exchange, unit of account, and insurer against loss
options.misconception: substitutes an insurance role for the store of value

questions.explanation: The three functions usually listed are the medium of exchange, which removes the need to barter; the unit of account, which gives prices a common denominator so amounts can be added; and the store of value, which lets purchasing power be carried across time. Production and income are what labour and capital supply rather than what money supplies, and distributing goods is the job of markets and retailers, not of the asset used to quote prices. Insurance is a real service, but it is bought in the market rather than provided by holding cash, so it does not displace the store of value.
questions.hint: Ask what money does for a transaction, a price, and next month.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: state what separates the narrow measure from the broad measure
questions.stem: A statistician reports currency in circulation of 800, checkable deposits of 1,700, savings deposits of 600, and small time deposits of 200. How should the two standard money measures differ?

options.text: The narrow measure takes currency and checkable deposits; the broad one adds the other two
The narrow measure takes deposits only; the broad one adds currency in circulation
options.misconception: believes the narrow measure excludes currency held by the public

options.text: The two differ only in whether deposits are netted against outstanding bank loans
options.misconception: believes the measures differ by netting rather than by inclusion

options.text: The broad one is always larger because it also counts currency in bank vaults
options.misconception: believes vault cash belongs to the broad measure but not the narrow one

questions.explanation: The narrow measure counts what can be spent straight away, so it is currency in circulation plus checkable deposits, 800 + 1,700 = 2,500. The broad measure adds balances that are spendable only after a transfer, so it also picks up the 600 of savings deposits and the 200 of small time deposits, giving 3,300. Neither measure nets loans against deposits; the broad one simply includes more tiers, and currency sitting in a bank's own vault has left the public's hands, so it is excluded from both.
questions.hint: Ask which balances can be spent without a transfer first.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: predict how nominal income moves currency demand
questions.stem: Holding currency pays nothing and costs something, so households carry it for transactions and for precaution. What happens to currency demand when nominal income rises, other conditions unchanged?

options.text: It rises, because the volume of transactions the household must make grows with income
It falls, because a richer household keeps a smaller share of its income in cash
options.misconception: believes cash holdings shrink as a share of a larger income

options.text: It is unchanged, because currency demand responds to prices rather than to income
options.misconception: believes money demand is driven only by the price level

options.text: It rises by more than income, because richer households hold proportionally more cash
options.misconception: believes the income response of currency demand is greater than one

questions.explanation: Money is wanted to carry out transactions, and a higher nominal income means a larger flow of receipts and payments to settle, so the balance a household finds it must hold rises with income. The standard specification makes the income response positive and less than one, since a richer household does hold proportionally less cash, but the level of cash still rises. Prices matter to money demand, yet the level of income matters too, and a response larger than income is not implied by anything in the transactions argument.
questions.hint: Ask what a larger income does to the number of payments to be made.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Currency demand and the interest rate
questions.learningObjective: predict how the interest rate moves currency demand
questions.stem: A household can hold a deposit that pays interest or hold currency that pays nothing. What happens to the household's demand for currency when the rate paid on deposits rises?

options.text: It falls, because holding currency forgoes a larger return on the deposit alternative
It rises, because a higher rate makes currency look safer next to a deposit
options.misconception: believes a higher deposit return makes currency more attractive

options.text: It is unchanged, because the interest rate never enters a money demand choice
options.misconception: believes the opportunity cost of holding cash is irrelevant

options.text: It rises, because a higher rate lifts the price level and with it cash holdings
options.misconception: links currency demand to prices rather than to the alternative return

questions.explanation: Currency earns nothing, so holding it costs exactly the return forgone on the best interest bearing alternative, and a higher deposit rate makes that cost larger and pushes demand for cash down. The same logic makes bonds a closer competitor to money, which is why money demand falls as interest rates rise. Prices do enter money demand, but the mechanism running here is the opportunity cost of liquidity, and a higher deposit rate certainly does not make non interest bearing currency look safer or more attractive.
questions.hint: Ask what holding cash costs once deposits pay more.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: state the expectation behind a liquidity preference holding
questions.stem: A household keeps cash in a drawer rather than in a deposit that pays interest. Under the liquidity preference motive, what is that household expecting to gain?

options.text: Immediate use at no delay and no cost once an uncertain need turns up
A higher return from currency than any interest paying deposit offers
options.misconception: believes non interest bearing currency out earns deposits

options.text: The ability to spend on goods that a deposit balance is not allowed to buy
options.misconception: believes currency buys a different set of goods from deposits

options.text: Freedom from paying tax on the interest a deposit account would have earned
options.misconception: believes the motive is avoiding interest income tax rather than liquidity

questions.explanation: Liquidity preference is the desire to hold wealth in a form that can be spent at once, without waiting for a transfer or paying a fee, and a drawer full of cash is the purest form of it. The household trades away interest income for that immediacy, which is a real cost, and it accepts that cost because the need it fears is uncertain. Currency pays nothing and buys nothing a deposit cannot buy, so the motive is about timing and certainty rather than about return, tax treatment, or access to a different set of goods.
questions.hint: Ask what the holder gives up and what they get instead.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: What a bank balance sheet shows
questions.learningObjective: judge what a single bank balance sheet can reveal about money
questions.stem: One bank's balance sheet lists deposits of 4,000, vault cash of 400, and loans of 3,700. What can legitimately be concluded about the money supply from that statement alone?

options.text: Only that this bank holds 400 of cash against 4,000 of deposits, and nothing wider
That the money supply is at least 7,700, since all three of its lines count as money
options.misconception: adds a bank's total assets as though each were part of the money stock

options.text: That deposits across the whole banking system cannot exceed 4,000 during the year
options.misconception: believes one bank's deposit line fixes the system wide total

options.text: That this bank has created 3,700 of new money since it began taking deposits
options.misconception: believes every loan a bank makes is a matching rise in the money supply

questions.explanation: A single bank's sheet is a private ledger, so it shows that this bank holds 400 of cash behind 4,000 of deposits, and it says nothing about the deposits other banks hold or about the size of the money stock overall. Adding the bank's own asset total double counts, because its loans are matched by deposits that already appear, and one bank's deposits are only a slice of the system wide figure. A loan creates a deposit, so part of the money stock does grow, but the deposit it creates is a transfer of purchasing power rather than new production, and the growth depends on reserves and on what the borrower does next.
questions.hint: Ask whether one bank's sheet can speak for the whole banking system.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Central bank balance sheet and open market operations
questions.learningObjective: trace an open market purchase on the central bank balance sheet
questions.stem: A central bank buys 400 of government bonds from dealers and credits the dealers' accounts held at the central bank. Which change follows on the central bank's own balance sheet?

options.text: Its bond holdings rise by 400 and its reserve liabilities rise by 400
Its bond holdings fall by 400 and its currency in circulation falls by 400
options.misconception: reverses both sides of the open market purchase

options.text: Its reserve liabilities fall by 400 and its bond holdings fall by 400
options.misconception: treats an open market purchase as a sale of bonds

options.text: Its total liabilities are unchanged, because credits to dealer accounts are not obligations
options.misconception: believes credits to dealer accounts are not central bank liabilities

questions.explanation: The central bank gives up bonds, which are assets, and receives a credit to the dealers' accounts, which are its liabilities, so the asset side rises by 400 and the liability side rises by 400 and the two sides still balance. The reserves those balances represent are the monetary base, so an open market purchase raises the base, which is why it is a conventional way of easing. The transaction is a purchase rather than a sale, and a credit to a dealer's account is plainly an obligation of the central bank to that dealer, so the liability side cannot stay where it was.
questions.hint: Ask which side of the sheet the bonds sit on and which side the credits sit on.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: name the components of the monetary base
questions.stem: Which pair of items together makes up the monetary base, on the definition generally used?

options.text: Currency in circulation outside the central bank, plus depository reserves at it
Currency in circulation, plus the central bank's own holdings of government bonds
options.misconception: substitutes central bank bond holdings for reserves at the central bank

options.text: Commercial bank loans to customers, plus the currency those banks hold in vault
options.misconception: substitutes bank lending and vault cash for the monetary base

options.text: The broad money stock, plus the central bank's holdings of foreign reserves
options.misconception: substitutes broad money and foreign assets for currency and reserves

questions.explanation: The base is the money the central bank itself has issued or holds on deposit, so it is currency in the hands of the public and banks, plus the reserves commercial banks and other depository institutions keep at the central bank. It deliberately excludes what the central bank holds in the way of assets, since government bonds are not part of the base even though a bond purchase changes its size. It also excludes bank lending and vault cash, which belong to the commercial banking system, and the broad money stock is a much larger aggregate built on top of the base rather than part of it.
questions.hint: Ask what the central bank has itself issued or holds as deposits.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: interpret the money multiplier that links base to money
questions.stem: A country's monetary base stands at 800 and its measured money multiplier is 3. What does that multiplier say about how a unit of base supports the money stock?

options.text: One unit of base supports three units of money, because deposits expand through lending
One unit of base supports three units of money, because banks must hold three in reserve
options.misconception: reverses the ratio and reads the multiplier as a reserve requirement

options.text: One unit of base turns into three units of currency held by the public
options.misconception: believes the multiplier converts base into currency rather than deposits

options.text: The money stock must be a third of the base, because reserve requirements bind
options.misconception: inverts the relationship between the base and the money stock

questions.explanation: The money multiplier is the money stock divided by the base, so 3 means the money stock of 2,400 rests on a base of 800. The mechanism is fractional reserve lending: a new deposit leaves a fraction as required reserve, the rest can be lent, and the loan gets redeposited, repeating until reserves or leakages stop the process. The multiplier is not a reserve requirement, which is the reciprocal of the simple version, and it is not a currency conversion, since the expansion runs mainly through deposits created by lending. The multiplier is also a ratio of a larger figure to a smaller one, so the money stock exceeds the base rather than falling short of it.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two figures the multiplier divides, and by which.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The quantity theory in its simplest form
questions.learningObjective: state the quantity equation and the prediction it makes
questions.stem: In its simplest form the quantity theory says that the money stock times the velocity of money equals the price level times real output. What does that equation predict for a lasting rise in the money stock?

options.text: The price level rises in the same proportion, if velocity and real output are unchanged
Real output rises in the same proportion, if prices and velocity are unchanged
options.misconception: believes money growth permanently enlarges real output instead

options.text: The price level is unchanged, because money is only a medium of exchange
options.misconception: believes neutral money can never drive a lasting rise in prices

options.text: The price level rises in the same proportion, even if velocity also rises
options.misconception: ignores the velocity term when predicting the effect

questions.explanation: With the velocity of money and real output both held fixed, the equation M x V = P x Y forces the price level to move in proportion to the money stock, so a 10 percent rise in M is a 10 percent rise in P. The equation is a statement about the level of prices rather than about the capacity to produce, so it does not make real output the variable that absorbs the increase. A rising velocity would amplify the effect rather than leaving it intact, which is why the prediction is conditional on velocity and real output both being unchanged.
questions.hint: Hold velocity and output fixed and see which variable must move.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compute the velocity of money from nominal output and money
questions.stem: In one year a country's nominal gross domestic product is 8,000 billion currency, and its money stock averaged 1,000 billion currency over that year. What is the velocity of money for the year, in times per year?
questions.explanation: Velocity is nominal output divided by the money stock, so 8,000 / 1,000 = 8 times per year, meaning the average unit of money is used in eight rounds of spending during the year. A second route reaches the same figure from the ratio of the two totals: the money stock is one eighth of nominal output, so each unit must circulate eight times for the total spending to reach that level. The assumptions are that the average money stock is the right divisor rather than a single date's balance, that the money stock is defined consistently with nominal output, and that the two series cover the same year.
questions.hint: Divide nominal output by the money stock, keeping both in the same units.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: derive money demand from income and the opportunity cost
questions.stem: Money demand rises with the transactions a person must carry out and falls with the return given up by not holding an interest bearing asset. Which conclusion follows from that logic?

options.text: Money demand rises with nominal income and falls with the interest rate
Money demand rises with the interest rate, since higher rates make households richer
options.misconception: believes the opportunity cost of money raises demand for it

options.text: Money demand moves with income and rates only while prices are rising
options.misconception: believes money demand needs an inflation trend to move at all

options.text: Money demand is set by the money stock, since the stock must always equal demand
options.misconception: believes the money stock determines demand rather than the reverse

questions.explanation: Both determinants in the standard specification are exactly these two: a positive term in nominal income, because a larger nominal flow of payments requires a larger balance, and a negative term in the interest rate, because holding money costs the return forgone on bonds and deposits. A higher rate makes a household's income from savings larger, not its demand for idle balances larger, so the sign on rates is negative rather than positive. The demand schedule holds whatever the price level happens to be doing, and equilibrium comes from supply of money meeting this demand, not from the other way round.
questions.hint: Ask what two variables enter the standard money demand function.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Money as store of value under inflation
questions.learningObjective: judge how high inflation affects money's store of value role
questions.stem: A country's inflation runs at 60 percent a year, and households must still settle their bills in currency. What happens to money's ability to serve as a store of value in that setting?

options.text: It erodes, because the real value of a fixed cash balance falls as prices rise
It improves, because lenders demand compensation before accepting a fixed nominal claim
options.misconception: believes high inflation raises the real value of a nominal claim

options.text: It is unchanged, because a promise to pay a fixed nominal sum never loses value
options.misconception: believes a fixed nominal promise preserves its real value under rising prices

options.text: It improves, because households will hold more currency to discharge the role of saving
options.misconception: believes holding more cash makes the store of value role stronger

questions.explanation: Cash is a fixed nominal claim, so at 60 percent inflation the same balance buys roughly two fifths as much a year later and its store of value role erodes fast, which is why households rush to spend or to convert balances into assets. Lenders do demand compensation, but that shows up in the interest rate they charge rather than in the real value of any particular nominal sum, and compensation is a separate matter from holding cash. More currency in circulation reflects a collapsing willingness to hold balances, not a stronger capacity to store value, so the diagnosis is erosion rather than improvement.
questions.hint: Ask what the same fixed balance buys after a year of 60 percent inflation.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: distinguish inflation from a one-off price movement
questions.stem: Prices of one category of goods jump sharply for a few months and then settle. Later the general price level rises for several years running. Which of these is inflation as the term is normally used?

options.text: The sustained rise in the general price level across the economy in the later period
The sharp rise in one category of prices during the first few months
options.misconception: equates a one-off sectoral price jump with general inflation

options.text: Both episodes equally, because inflation is any increase in any single price
options.misconception: believes any price increase of any size counts as inflation

options.text: Neither episode, because inflation can only be measured against a base year
options.misconception: denies that inflation can be measured at all

questions.explanation: Inflation is a continuing rise in the general level of prices, which is a statement about the price level as a whole over a period, and the later episode is that. A sharp move in one category is a relative price change and may simply be offset elsewhere, so it is not by itself inflation, and the term does not cover any increase in any price however small. A base year is a convenient reference for measuring the level, not a precondition for the phenomenon, so neither episode is disqualified by how it would be indexed.
questions.hint: Ask whether the price level itself moved, and for how long.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: state the Fisher equation in its exact form
questions.stem: The Fisher equation links a nominal interest rate to a real rate and expected inflation. In which form is it properly written?

options.text: One plus the nominal rate equals one plus the real rate times one plus inflation
The nominal rate is the real rate less expected inflation, so inflation lowers it
options.misconception: reverses the sign and the direction of the relation

options.text: The nominal rate is the real rate plus expected inflation, with no factorisation
options.misconception: states the linear approximation as though it were an identity

options.text: One plus the nominal rate equals one plus the real rate added to one plus inflation
options.misconception: adds the two factors instead of multiplying them

questions.explanation: The exact relation multiplies the two gross factors, (1 + nominal) = (1 + real) x (1 + expected inflation), so a one percent real return on a sum that itself keeps its purchasing power is not the same as a one percent rise in prices. Dropping the cross product gives the familiar approximation that the nominal rate is the real rate plus expected inflation, which is close for small rates but is not the equation itself, and the sign is positive rather than negative, since expected inflation raises the nominal rate a lender must be paid. The two factors are multiplied, never added, because they apply successively to the same sum.
questions.hint: Ask whether inflation and the real return apply one after the other or together.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: explain why the real rate differs from the nominal rate
questions.stem: A lender is paid a 9 percent nominal rate on a one-year loan, and inflation over that year turns out to be 6 percent. What was the real return, and why does the difference matter?

options.text: About 2.8 percent, so part of the nominal return only replaced lost purchasing power
About 15 percent, because the two rates should be added to obtain the real return
options.misconception: believes the real return is the sum of the nominal rate and inflation

options.text: Exactly 3 percent, because the real rate is the nominal rate less inflation
options.misconception: believes the exact real rate is the simple difference of the two rates

options.text: About 0.5 percent, because inflation should be subtracted from the real rate itself
options.misconception: subtracts inflation from the real rate rather than the nominal rate

questions.explanation: The real return is the exact ratio (1 + 0.09) / (1 + 0.06) - 1 = 1.09 / 1.06 - 1 = 0.0283, so about 2.8 percent, and the lender bought back roughly two thirds of the lender's original purchasing power. Subtracting to get exactly 3 percent is the linear approximation, which is close but not exact once the rates are of this size, and it is the exact figure that determines whether anyone borrowed or saved. The distinction matters because a 9 percent nominal return that is 6 percent inflation is a losing proposition in real terms, and it is also the distinction that lets a nominal rate rise while the real rate falls.
questions.hint: Ask what the lender's repayment buys at the year's end prices.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: identify the mechanism of demand pull inflation
questions.stem: An economy is producing close to capacity, and spending rises faster than the supply of goods and services can respond. What is the resulting price increase called, and why does it happen?

Cost push inflation, because wage and input costs rise to meet the extra demand

options.text: Cost push inflation, because a currency appreciation makes imported goods dearer

options.text: Demand pull inflation, because a rise in the money stock shrinks real output
options.misconception: attributes demand pull inflation to a contraction of output

questions.explanation: With output near its capacity, extra spending cannot call forth extra supply, so the adjustment happens in price: competing buyers bid prices up and that is demand pull inflation. Cost push inflation runs the other way, from a rise in costs to the price of output, so mislabelling this episode would point the analysis at the wrong shock. An appreciating currency is not what is described here at all, and money growth does not shrink real output, so neither of those belongs in the causal chain of a spending surge at capacity.

questions.learningObjective: identify the mechanism of cost push inflation
questions.stem: A sharp rise in world oil prices feeds into transport, food, and heating costs across an economy, and firms pass those higher costs on in the prices they charge. What is this episode called?

A single input can be important enough to move the general level, and a cost shock pushes prices up rather than down, so the deflation reading has the direction backwards as well as the cause.

questions.learningObjective: explain why core and headline measures can diverge

questions.learningObjective: compute the ex post real interest rate from a deflated return
questions.stem: A one-year deposit pays 7 percent nominal. Over that year the consumer price index rises 4 percent, from 100 to 104. What is the real return on the deposit, in percent to two decimal places?

A second route back-substitutes into the deposit itself: one unit deposited grows to 1.07, and at the year's end prices that buys 1.07 / 1.04 = 1.028846 units of the base period basket, so the purchasing power grew by 2.8846 percent. questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Why the quantity equation predicts nothing
questions.learningObjective: explain why an identity carries no predictive content
questions.stem: Explain why the quantity equation can hold exactly while the version of the quantity theory that assumes constant velocity fails to predict the rate of inflation.

answer.exemplar: The equation M x V = P x Y is an identity: the left side and the right side are two ways of measuring the same nominal spending, so it cannot be violated, and any of the four quantities can always be solved for once the other three are known. That is also why it has no forecasting power. A prediction needs a law for one of the terms, and the version that assumes velocity constant supplies none: in a year when money grew 25 percent, output 12 percent, and prices 5 percent, the equation forces velocity to fall by 5.92 percent, and a constant velocity figure of 1.25 divided by 1.12 would have predicted 11.6 percent inflation instead of 5. The equation was satisfied throughout; the 5.92 percent velocity move is the whole explanation, and because velocity responds to the money growth it is meant to explain, the assumption is exactly what is missing. The content of the quantity theory therefore lies in a theory of velocity or of money demand, not in the equation.

questions.explanation: A model answer must separate the identity from the behavioural assumption and show the velocity move numerically, because the common error is to think the equation itself failed when the prediction did.
questions.hint: Ask what is guaranteed by the accounting and what has to be assumed about velocity.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: What indexation can and cannot do
questions.learningObjective: explain the limits of wage indexation against inflation
questions.stem: Explain what full indexation of wages to a price index does to the distribution of the cost of inflation, and what it leaves untouched.

answer.exemplar: With full indexation the nominal wage rises by exactly the index, 30.00 becoming 30.00 x 1.045 = 31.35 when the index rises 4.5 percent, so the real wage is unchanged at 1.0225 divided by 1.045, which is 1. What indexation removes is therefore the arbitrary loss of purchasing power that a fixed nominal wage suffers when prices rise, and with it the distributional question of which workers bear the first period of an inflation, since nobody's real wage depends on the timing of the adjustment. Half indexation cuts that loss to 1.0225 divided by 1.045 = 0.9785, a fall of 2.15 percent, so partial coverage shares the burden rather than removing it. What indexation does not do is touch the aggregate real cost of the inflation: the goods and services the economy produces still cost more real resources than before, that burden now appears as a smaller money wage rate rather than as a lower nominal wage, and 2.25 percent of productivity gains being paid out in nominal wage growth is still 2.25 percent of them gone.

questions.explanation: A model answer must distinguish the distributional effect, which indexation removes, from the aggregate real cost, which it only relabels, because treating indexation as a free lunch is the error the question targets.
questions.hint: Separate the effect on who bears the shock from the effect on the total real cost.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: explain the debt channel that amplifies deflation
questions.stem: Explain how a fall in the price level can deepen an economic downturn rather than simply reversing an earlier rise.

answer.exemplar: A fall in the price level leaves the money value of debts fixed, so a loan of 10,000 becomes 10,000 / 0.95 = 10,526 of purchasing power after a 5 percent deflation, a 5.26 percent rise in what is actually owed. Debtors then cut spending to service the larger real burden, which lowers demand further and lowers prices again, while creditors become more cautious and asset prices fall faster than the general level, tightening collateral and curbing the new lending that recovery needs. Real balances rise as prices fall, which normally should support spending, but the debt channel can outweigh that effect, which is why the same price decline that was supposed to help lenders and borrowers in reverse ends up prolonging the weakness. Expectations reinforce it: anticipating further declines leads firms to postpone investment and households to postpone purchases, and that anticipation is itself a cause of the next decline rather than a report of it.

questions.explanation: A model answer must show the real debt burden rising with a worked figure and then trace the spending and collateral consequences, because the point is a mechanism that amplifies rather than merely reverses.
questions.hint: Ask what a fixed nominal debt is worth after prices fall.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: explain the feedback from expectations to realised inflation
questions.stem: Explain how an inflation expectation that is not anchored can generate the inflation it anticipates, and what breaks the loop.

answer.exemplar: The loop runs through pricing. If workers expect 6 percent inflation, they set wage demands 6 percent above the current rate; that raises firms' unit costs, so firms raise prices 6 percent; and the realised price rise is then 6 percent, exactly what was expected, with no policy or shock required. Because each round is justified by the previous one, nothing in the process pulls the rate back, and a second round built on the first can add another 6 percent on the new base. What breaks the loop is a long run anchor: a stated and credible price level target, or a monetary authority's commitment to a stable money growth rate, gives both sides an expected rate that differs from the one they are currently extrapolating, so wage and price decisions are pulled toward it rather than compounding the last round. Credibility is what does the work, since an uncredible anchor changes nothing.

questions.explanation: A model answer must trace the chain from expectation through wages to prices back to the realised rate, and must state that the loop is broken by a credible anchor rather than by a target on its own.
questions.hint: Follow one round from the expectation to the price change it produces.
